_readme: Every fact the pages print comes from here. Unknown stays null - the pages render a gap, never a guess. Hazard wording comes from the in-game 'What if...' banners as recorded in creator footage (Votex, 2026-10-19; VendoPlus via AllThingsHow, 2026-10-20). Survival notes are guidance derived from that hazard behaviour, not developer statements.

codesFaq.q: Does What If Disasters have codes?
codesFaq.a: Not yet. Every round we re-check the lobby, the group shout and the developer's socials; nothing has been released as of 25 October 2026. The game's lobby buttons are SHOP, MISSIONS and INDEX - no codes button is documented.

codesFaq.q: Why do people search for What If Disasters codes?
codesFaq.a: Because almost every Roblox game has them. This one hands out rewards through missions, crates and credits instead. If the developer adds a code box, the first working code goes on this page the same day it is confirmed by two sources.

codesFaq.q: What can I get for free right now?
codesFaq.a: Nothing that needs a code - credits come from surviving rounds, and the lobby crates take credits. The Robux game passes are a paid shortcut, not a requirement.

codesFaq.q: How often is this page checked?
codesFaq.a: On every game update. The page footer shows the date of the last check, and an empty list means the game still has no codes.

entities.name: The Moon Falls
entities.summary: The moon drops toward Earth in stages. The sea first surges in and out, burning chunks fall from the sky, and gravity weakens until loose objects and players start lifting off the ground.
entities.howToGet: Get indoors before the surge reaches the shoreline and stay under a roof while debris falls. Sitting out the whole scenario in the open is what kills most rounds of this one.
entities.banner: What if the moon falls?
stages: Moon approaches — HUD reads DISTANCE TO THE MOON: 310,000 KM and the prompt is GET SOMEWHERE SAFE.
Tides rise — TIDE HEIGHT +20 METERS and still climbing past +50, with the prompt switching to GET SOMEWHERE HIGH.
Ground splits — EARTHQUAKES ARE STARTING, so the threat comes from below while the water is still up.
Moon breaks up — THE MOON IS CRACKING APART — falling burning debris adds a threat from above.
entities.killSpots: The streets once the tide passes +20 m, and anything at ground level when the earthquakes start. The stage prompt is the tell: the moment it changes from SAFE to HIGH, low ground stops being survivable.
prep: Climb before the tide stage — two-storey houses with stairs, car roofs and bus-stop shelters all work as height.
Pick a spot with a roof as well as height: the last stage drops burning debris.
Do not stay in the street to watch the distance readout fall. The water arrives while you are reading it.
entities.ifCaught: Move inland and under a roof in the same run — stopping to watch the wave from a rooftop puts you back under the debris. If you are already lifting off the ground, get to a wall and stay against it.
entities.worstMaps: Coastal Resort and Harbor Port — the surge phase reaches further inland and the low decks offer no roof cover.
entities.hud: The distance readout falls from DISTANCE TO THE MOON: 310,000 KM toward 8,402 KM as the round runs, and the stage text names what is coming rather than what is happening.

entities.name: THE SUN DISAPPEARS
entities.summary: A permanent deep freeze sets in while the power grid fails. The map goes dark and cold rather than being torn apart, so the round is lost to exposure in the open rather than to one big hit.
entities.howToGet: Treat it as a shelter round: find an interior and stay in it for the full timer. Running between buildings to loot is what gets players caught outside when the freeze deepens.
entities.banner: What if the sun disappears?
stages: The light goes out. The map turns dark enough that you lose track of where the streets run.
The deep freeze sets in while the power grid fails, so the buildings that looked like shelter stop being lit or powered.
The cold keeps deepening for the rest of the round rather than hitting once, so exposure is the thing that finishes the round.
entities.killSpots: Anywhere outside. This scenario does not tear the map apart, so the losing move is choosing to keep moving between buildings instead of committing to one.
prep: Pick one interior and get inside it before the banner ends.
Learn the door you came in through — moving in the dark is where people get lost.
Do not plan a route that needs street time later in the round. The cold gets worse, not better.
entities.ifCaught: Break line of sight to the open sky and get inside the nearest building, even one you did not plan on. A worse shelter beats a better one you never reach.
entities.worstMaps: Any map with long exposed crossings — the Golden Gate crossing has the most unavoidable outdoor distance between covers.
entities.hud: The panel tracks power on the bar (43% ONLINE in the recorded round): the grid shutting down is what turns the round cold.

entities.name: A 500 m Mega Tsunami
entities.summary: A wave that grows as it approaches and drags players off the coast. The water arrives later than the warning does, so the 30-second head start is the entire survival window.
entities.howToGet: Climb first and loot never. Second floors, roofs and hillside ledges are the only ground that stays dry; anything at street level gets swept.
entities.banner: What if a 500 m mega tsunami hits?
stages: The water pulls back first, which is the only warning you get.
The wave builds as it approaches, so the height at the shoreline is not the height that arrives.
It drags players off the coast rather than hitting once — the wash-out is as dangerous as the impact.
entities.killSpots: Street level on every coastal map, and every low roof. The wave grows on approach, so a first-floor rooftop that survives the first seconds may not survive the pass.
prep: Climb immediately — second floor, roof ridge, or hillside ledge above the waterfront.
Aim inland as well as up: height inland beats height on the shoreline.
Do not spend the 30 seconds looting the beach. The wave is the round.
entities.ifCaught: Go up anything, even a car roof, and keep climbing if the water reaches you. Being swept is the failure state — you do not recover from it.
entities.worstMaps: Coastal Resort and Harbor Port — the low waterfront is most of the playable area.

entities.name: Earth Enters a Mega Storm
entities.summary: A storm that tracks wind speed as it builds — the HUD climbs toward 150 KM/H — and then starts roping out tornadoes. The banner's own name for the late stage is that the storm never ends.
entities.howToGet: Get indoors before the wind speed peaks and stay there. The tornadoes that rope out in the late stages are the part that removes whatever cover you picked, so keep a second building in mind.
entities.banner: What if Earth enters a mega storm?
stages: Wind speed starts climbing and the HUD tracks it — recorded rounds reach 150 KM/H.
Loose props start moving and open ground becomes a losing position before the tornadoes even appear.
Tornadoes rope out of the storm, and the late stage is described as a storm that never ends.
entities.killSpots: Open ground while the wind builds, and any building on the path of a roped-out tornado. Players die trying to cross to a better building after the wind is already up.
prep: Get inside early — the wind stage is survivable outdoors, the tornado stage is not.
Prefer a solid building over a shelter made of props; loose objects become projectiles.
Note a second building nearby, because the first can be taken by a tornado.
entities.ifCaught: Move between buildings in short runs and hug the wall on the way. Crossing the open in one go is the mistake that ends rounds here.
entities.worstMaps: Thrill Park — the map this scenario was recorded on, with long open walkways between structures.
entities.hud: The storm readout counts strikes per minute — 240 PER MINUTE in the recorded round, with the stage text warning that anything stood still gets struck too.

entities.name: EARTH FREEZES OVER
entities.summary: Snow starts falling and the temperature keeps dropping until the oceans freeze solid. Buildings give out from the cold rather than from a wave, so the round is a shelter round with collapsing cover.
entities.howToGet: Get into a building and stay in the warmest corner. Recorded rounds survived by not moving at all — the buildings that fall are the ones people leave.
entities.banner: What if Earth completely froze?
stages: Snow starts falling on a map that would never normally see it, and the HUD switches to finding shelter.
So cold that buildings begin to fail — structures collapse on their own, not because anything hit them.
The oceans freeze solid — the end state, where anything not indoors is done.
entities.killSpots: Outdoors, and inside a building that is already failing. The damage comes from being exposed when a structure gives out, so standing under a cracking roof is not shelter.
prep: Pick a solid interior, not an open or damaged one.
Stay in one warm corner instead of moving between buildings.
Do not go exploring for a better building once the snow starts.
entities.ifCaught: Get inside the nearest intact building and stay put. Moving again after you are inside is what gets players caught when a structure comes down.
entities.worstMaps: Open maps with flimsy structures — Jungle Pyramids and the Golden Gate crossing.
entities.hud: The stage panel reads THE SUN IS FADING — the thick air is freezing and sunlight can no longer reach the ground.

entities.name: The Atmosphere Disappears
entities.role: Any map, windows and open air
entities.summary: Windows break, the wind tears loose everything not fixed, the sun burns without protection and the oceans boil. With no air pressure there is no sound, which removes the usual audio warning.
entities.howToGet: Find a sealed room. A car does not count, and a room with broken windows does not count — the survival recorded was in an interior with the glass still intact.
entities.banner: What if Earth lost its atmosphere?
stages: The wind picks up and everything loose starts flying — the first sign that the air itself is the hazard.
Windows break and the sky darkens; unprotected exposure burns, and the oceans start boiling.
The round settles into the end state: no atmosphere, no sound, nothing safe outside.
entities.killSpots: Anywhere without intact glass between you and the outside: streets, roofs, and cars. Players die by treating a vehicle as shelter.
prep: Find a room with unbroken windows before the wind stage.
Do not use a car — recorded rounds show it does nothing.
Stay away from the windows once inside; they are the thing that fails.
entities.ifCaught: Run for the nearest interior with intact glass and close the door behind you. If the windows in your building are already gone, move to another one before the burning stage.
entities.worstMaps: The Golden Gate crossing has almost no interior, and the deck is fully exposed.
entities.hud: The recorded stage text is THE OCEAN IS BOILING — the seas boiling away and the exposed seabed scorching — so the ground you are standing on changes twice.

entities.name: Rain for 1,000 Years
entities.summary: The rain does not stop. The HUD counts the downpour forward by months and then years while the water level climbs, until the map is an island and pieces of it break off.
entities.howToGet: Get to the highest ground immediately and expect it to be submerged anyway — the recorded survival came from staying on top of a structure while the water and the structure both failed around it.
entities.banner: What if it rained for 1,000 years?
stages: The counter starts at MONTH 1 and the HUD reads MONTH 10 within the round: whole neighbourhoods under water and lightning through the endless storm.
The objective is FIND THE TALLEST BUILDING, NOW — the game tells you height is the answer before the streets flood.
The counter keeps running toward years while the map loses pieces; what is left at the end is an island.
entities.killSpots: Low ground at any point, and swimming distance from a structure once the water is up. The water keeps rising slowly enough that players underestimate it.
prep: Climb before the counter reaches months — not after the streets flood.
Pick a structure with a top you can stand on, not just a roof you can be under.
Do not plan to swim; the recorded round ends with the map itself breaking apart.
entities.ifCaught: Climb the nearest structure and keep climbing as pieces break off. Staying on a submerging surface is the same as staying in the water.
entities.worstMaps: Suburban Neighborhood and Coastal Resort — low buildings with limited height.
entities.hud: The counter runs MONTH 10 → years, with a depth readout in metres (1.5 METERS in the recorded round) and the objective FIND THE TALLEST BUILDING, NOW.

entities.name: Yellowstone Erupts
entities.summary: A single supervolcano rather than the every-volcano round: the surface turns toxic, a wall of ash moves across the map, and the heat arrives with it. Underground sealed space is the only cover that works.
entities.howToGet: Get into a sealed underground space — a bunker — before the eruption reaches the map. A normal building is not enough once the ash cloud arrives.
entities.banner: What if Yellowstone erupted?
stages: The eruption starts and the air outside turns toxic — being outdoors becomes damage.
An ash cloud moves across the map, bringing heat with it.
The surface stays lethal for the rest of the round, so anything above ground is lost.
entities.killSpots: The surface at any point after the eruption: streets, roofs and ordinary buildings. Players die by coming back up to look.
prep: Find the bunker or underground space during the first stage, before the ash arrives.
Do not come back up to watch the cloud — the recorded death was on the stairs.
Treat the roof as gone for the whole round, not just for the blast.
entities.ifCaught: Get underground and stay there. The round is decided by whether you had sealed space, not by how you move once the cloud is overhead.
entities.worstMaps: Maps without underground space excepted — Jungle Pyramids has the most sheltered ground of the recorded maps.
entities.hud: After the eruption the panel reads YELLOWSTONE HAS ERUPTED: ash raining on the whole map and the ground rumbling, with STAY UNDER A ROOF as the objective.

entities.name: Earth Spins Backwards
entities.summary: The planet reverses its rotation. Recorded rounds show the storms reversing direction with it, which means the safe side of a wind hazard is the opposite of the one you learned.
entities.howToGet: Do not rely on the direction a storm was tracking before the banner — after the reversal, the side you are standing on may be the exposed one. Re-read the map when the reversal hits.
entities.banner: What if Earth spins backwards?
stages: The rotation reverses and the HUD reports it as the scenario starting.
Weather already on the map reverses direction with the planet — recorded footage notes every storm reversing.
From there the round plays out with the wind coming from the opposite side, so old cover positions are wrong.
entities.killSpots: Whatever position you picked for a wind hazard before the reversal. The hazard itself is familiar; the direction is inverted.
prep: Do not commit to a wind shelter before the banner names this scenario.
Once the reversal is announced, re-check which side of your cover is now exposed.
Assume anything that was sheltering you from wind is now doing the opposite.
entities.ifCaught: Move to the other side of whatever you were hiding behind. The same object is cover or exposure depending on which direction the wind is now coming from.
entities.worstMaps: Open maps where the only cover has one side — the Golden Gate crossing and Jungle Pyramids.

entities.name: Planet Flyby
entities.summary: Another planet passes close enough to lift the map off the ground. Chunks of the city rise toward it and towers start to fall, so the counter-intuitive answer is the recorded prompt: stay down low.
entities.howToGet: Stay low and indoors. Everything that gets pulled is what is above ground, so a basement, a low interior or the floor of a structure is the position — climbing is what gets you lifted.
entities.banner: What if another planet passed Earth?
stages: The planet appears and the HUD panel reads THE GROUND IS TEARING LOOSE: chunks of the city lifting off toward it, towers starting to fall.
The objective switches to STAY DOWN LOW — the only scenario in the game where the escape is downward.
Debris keeps rising for the rest of the round, so anything you climb onto becomes a projectile.
entities.killSpots: Rooftops, upper floors and anything already loose. Players die by climbing for a better view while the ground is being pulled upward.
prep: Get to the lowest interior you can reach before the pull starts.
Get off any rooftop — height is the hazard here, not the shelter.
Avoid standing under towers: the recorded stage description is that towers start to fall as the chunks lift.
entities.ifCaught: Get down a level and inside. Running for a taller building is the failure move; the round rewards the only prompt that tells you to go low.
entities.worstMaps: Venice (the recorded map) and any map with a lot of vertical structure — Alpine Ski Resort and Jungle Temple Ruins.

entities.name: The Sandstorm
entities.summary: A dust storm that turns the open ground toxic. The HUD adds DRY LIGHTNING on top — static crackling through the dust and starting fires — so the round is a shelter round with fire outside it.
entities.howToGet: Get inside and stay inside. The recorded prompt is STAY INSIDE, and the ground itself is described as too toxic to step on, so a roof matters more than a route.
entities.banner: What if the ocean vanished?
stages: Dust rolls in and the stage text reads DRY LIGHTNING: static crackling through the dust and igniting fires.
The ground becomes toxic to stand on, so running between buildings costs health even before the fires spread.
The fires started by the lightning keep burning through the round, which is what makes staying put inside the only stable answer.
entities.killSpots: Any open ground, and the gaps between buildings. Players die trying to move to a better shelter once the dust is up and the fires have started.
prep: Pick a building and commit during the 30 seconds — STAY INSIDE is the whole strategy.
Do not plan a route that needs street time once the lightning starts.
Watch for fires near your building: the round adds them, so the shelter can be lost from outside.
entities.ifCaught: Get into the nearest interior, even a poor one. Crossing open dust to reach a better building is how this round kills.
entities.worstMaps: Alpine Ski Resort (the recorded map) and other open maps with long gaps between buildings.

entities.name: The Witching Hour
entities.summary: The map goes dark and black thorns burst up out of the street and straight through the buildings. It is the round the game's own Halloween crate is named after, and the recorded prompt is simply to run.
entities.howToGet: Keep moving and stay out of the streets. The thorns come up through the ground and through structures, so standing still — indoors or not — is what gets you.
entities.banner: What if the witching hour came?
stages: The map drops into night and the HUD stage reads THORNS: BURSTING FROM THE GROUND.
Black vines spear up out of the street and straight through the buildings, so cover stops being cover.
The prompt is RUN FOR YOUR LIFE for the rest of the round — the hazard keeps coming up under wherever you stopped.
entities.killSpots: Standing still anywhere, and especially in the street. Unlike a debris or flood round, hiding inside does not help: the recorded stage description says the vines go through buildings.
prep: Pick a route rather than a hiding spot during the 30 seconds.
Get off the street — the vines come up through it first.
Keep moving once it starts; stopping to watch a vine line is how players get caught.
entities.ifCaught: Run, and change direction rather than backing into a corner. There is no shelter that holds for the whole round here.
entities.worstMaps: Downtown City (the recorded map) — dense streets with lots of ground for the vines to come up through.

entities.name: Oxygen Doubles
entities.summary: Twice the oxygen turns any spark into a firestorm: the HUD tracks FIRE SPREAD SPEED at 6.2× normal in the recorded round, fire runs along the ground and up the vines, and black smoke rolls down the streets.
entities.howToGet: Get upstairs and stay there. The recorded objective is STAY UPSTAIRS with a temperature readout — the fire owns the ground floor, so height is the answer for once.
entities.banner: What if there was twice as much oxygen?
stages: The HUD starts tracking fire spread speed — 6.2× normal in the recorded round.
Fire runs along the ground and climbs the vines, and black smoke rolls down the streets.
The round keeps the objective on STAY UPSTAIRS while the temperature readout climbs.
entities.killSpots: Ground level and anything connected to it. The smoke is the part people miss — it comes down the streets rather than up.
prep: Find stairs or a ramp during the 30 seconds — upper floors are the whole strategy.
Do not plan to cross the street level later in the round.
Watch the temperature readout: it tells you how close the fire front is.
entities.ifCaught: Climb, even to a worse building, rather than running at ground level. Staying upstairs is the only prompt this round gives.
entities.worstMaps: Stadium District (the recorded map) and Downtown City — dense buildings the fire front travels between.
entities.hud: Besides FIRE SPREAD SPEED 6.2× NORMAL, the HUD tracks temperature on the same bar — 48 °C in the recorded round.

entities.name: An Earthquake Sequence
entities.summary: A sequence rather than a single quake: a foreshock, then the main event at magnitude 10, then aftershocks. Buildings come down, so height stops being protection the way it is in a water round.
entities.howToGet: Get out of tall buildings before the main quake and stay in the open away from falling structures. This is the scenario that punishes the climb-first habit built by tsunami rounds.
entities.banner: What if an earthquake sequence hits?
stages: A foreshock shakes the map — the warning, not the event.
The main quake reads Magnitude 10 on the HUD and buildings start coming down.
Aftershocks continue while the damaged structures finish collapsing.
entities.killSpots: Inside or underneath tall buildings, and the top floors of anything that falls. Being high up is the worst position here.
prep: Get out of the tall building during the foreshock, not after the main quake.
Pick open ground that is not directly beside a facade — glass and walls come down outward.
Stay off rooftops entirely for this one.
entities.ifCaught: Run for open ground on the foreshock and do not go back inside for anything. If you are on a roof when the magnitude reads, get down the outside rather than waiting for the stairs.
entities.worstMaps: Dense city maps — Suburban Neighborhood's two-storey houses and Alpine Ski Resort's structures both shed debris.
entities.hud: The magnitude readout sits on the bar (21 in the recorded round) with the stage text A STRONG TREMOR IS SHAKING THIS TOWN — the number climbs, so you can read how far along the sequence is.

entities.name: The Biggest Bomb Ever Detonated
entities.summary: A single detonation rather than a building hazard: the round is about where the bomb lands and what you have between you and it. Recorded rounds show the blast being survivable behind solid cover.
entities.howToGet: Get hard cover between you and the detonation — a building, a wall, a vehicle — and stay behind it. Distance alone does not seem to be enough; the recorded survival was behind something sturdy.
entities.banner: What if the biggest bomb ever detonated?
stages: The bomb position is set — players start asking where it will go off, which is the only information available.
The detonation hits and anything without cover between it and the player is exposed.
The blast wave and aftermath are what the round is decided on; there is no second hit to prepare for.
entities.killSpots: Open ground anywhere in line of sight of the detonation. Standing on a roof counts as open ground here.
prep: Find a solid wall or building and put it between you and the open skyline.
Get off anything elevated — height gives no protection from a blast.
Do not wait to see where it lands before moving; move to cover first.
entities.ifCaught: Get behind the heaviest thing you can reach, even if it is a vehicle, and stay low. Running into the open to watch is the failure move.
entities.worstMaps: Maps with long sightlines and little solid cover — the Golden Gate crossing and Jungle Pyramids.
entities.hud: DISTANCE TO DETONATION counts down in kilometres (3 KM in the recorded round) and the prompt is HIDE BEHIND A WALL — distance alone is not the answer.

entities.name: Toxic Air
entities.summary: The air outside turns toxic. Players caught in the open report inhaling gas, which makes this a shelter round rather than a damage race — indoors is the whole answer.
entities.howToGet: Get indoors and stay indoors. Unlike the wind and water scenarios there is no partial answer: being outside at any point in the round is the damage.
entities.banner: What if the air turns toxic?
stages: The air turns toxic outside — the first sign is damage in the open rather than a visible hazard.
Anyone still outdoors keeps taking it, so a short trip becomes a losing trade.
The round stays that way to the end — cover does not expire, unlike a tornado or a rising tide.
entities.killSpots: Any outdoor space, including rooftops and streets. Players die trying to move to a better building after the air has already turned.
prep: Pick a building and commit before the banner — this is a sun-disappears round with a different cause.
Do not plan a route that needs street time later in the round.
Treat a car as outdoor space, because it is.
entities.ifCaught: Get into the nearest interior, even a poor one. Once inside, stay there rather than trading up for a better building.
entities.worstMaps: Maps with few interiors — the Golden Gate crossing has the least indoor space of the recorded maps.

entities.name: The Ocean Rolls Back
entities.summary: The sea pulls away from the coast before it comes back. The dry seabed is the bait: the water returns faster than anyone can cross it.
entities.howToGet: When the shoreline empties, go up instead of out to look. Walking onto the seabed is the mistake this scenario is built around.
entities.banner: What if the ocean rolls back?
stages: The sea empties out, exposing the seabed. It looks like new ground to explore.
The water returns faster than a player can cross the distance they just walked.
Anyone on the seabed when it comes back is beyond rescue — the round is decided there.
entities.killSpots: The exposed seabed. It is the bait of the scenario, and the fastest way to lose a round that otherwise has no hazard at all.
prep: When the shoreline empties, treat it as a warning, not an opening.
Move inland and up instead of out toward the water.
Keep other players in view — the temptation to follow someone onto the seabed is how groups get wiped.
entities.ifCaught: Drop everything and run inland; do not try to grab one more thing off the exposed ground. If the water is already returning, climb rather than outrun.
entities.worstMaps: Coastal Resort, Harbor Port and the Golden Gate crossing — all three have long shoreline or deck runs.

entities.name: The Floor Is Lava
entities.summary: Touching the ground burns, and the lava keeps rising as the round goes on. Height is the only currency: whatever you are standing on now will be submerged first.
entities.howToGet: Start moving upward before the first burn tick, and keep switching to the next surface up. Standing still on a roof only works until the level reaches it.
entities.banner: What if the floor becomes lava?
stages: The ground starts burning on contact — the first tick is a warning, not a death.
The lava keeps rising, which means every surface has a shelf life.
The map compresses upward until the highest point is the only place left.
entities.killSpots: Standing still on a surface that already started burning, and re-descending for loot after you climbed.
prep: Map your route upward during the 30 seconds, including a second surface above the first.
Do not commit to a roof that has no higher step — the rising level takes it.
Keep moving between surfaces rather than waiting for the burn to reach you.
entities.ifCaught: Take the burn for one step up rather than two steps sideways. Height resets the clock; distance does not.
entities.worstMaps: Flat maps are the worst — Suburban Neighborhood has the most ground to lose and the fewest high structures.

entities.name: Zombie Outbreak
entities.summary: Zombies smash through doors, players who die get back up infected, and fast red-glowing crawlers join later in the round. The threat is other players turning, not just the first wave.
entities.howToGet: Keep a door between you and the street, and never stand next to someone who is about to go down - the infected turn fast. Open ground with a group is worse than a closed room alone.
entities.banner: What if a zombie outbreak happens?
stages: Zombies start breaking through doors instead of waiting outside them.
Players who die get back up infected, so the crowd turns against itself as the round goes on.
Fast red-glowing crawlers join later, which is when holding a doorway stops working.
entities.killSpots: Doorways and groups. A door buys time against the first wave and nothing against crawlers, and standing beside someone who is about to turn is how a safe room becomes a death trap.
prep: Pick a room with one entrance and a second way out.
Keep space from other players instead of clustering at the door.
Count the crawlers when they appear — that is the signal to abandon the room, not defend it harder.
entities.ifCaught: Leave the room before the crawlers box you in. Running into the street is survivable; being cornered indoors is not.
entities.worstMaps: Suburban Neighborhood — enclosed houses with single doors are the trap, and the streets give crawlers room to run.
entities.hud: The objective counts infected inside your shelter — STAY UNDER A ROOF (×8) in the recorded round — and the prompt with it is GET HIGH, NOW: they spread faster than you can run.

entities.name: Earth Tilts 90 Degrees
entities.summary: Walls become floors and the sea drops onto the coasts. Anything that was a vertical surface is now walkable, and everything that was standing falls with the map.
entities.howToGet: Expect to be thrown: stay away from ledges, glass and anything loose while the tilt happens. Once the world settles, walk the old walls like ordinary ground.
entities.banner: What if Earth tilts 90°?
stages: The whole map rotates. Walls become floors and everything standing falls with the terrain.
Sea water drops onto the coasts as the oceans settle into their new orientation.
What counts as a safe height changes entirely — the old roof may now be a wall.
entities.killSpots: Ledges and glass during the rotation, and anything loose that falls with you. The tilt kills through the fall, not through a hazard chasing you.
prep: Stand away from ledges, windows and stacked props when the timer runs out.
Expect to be thrown and plan to land on something rather than to stay standing.
After the world settles, re-read the map — vertical surfaces are ordinary ground now.
entities.ifCaught: Do not fight the fall. Once it stops, walk the new floors instead of trying to reach the old ones.
entities.worstMaps: Tall, dense maps — Alpine Ski Resort and Jungle Pyramids both have a lot of vertical structure to fall through.
entities.hud: The stage text reads THE OCEANS ARE SLOSHING as the terrain rolls, which is the tell that the water is about to arrive from a direction it never came from before.

entities.name: EVERY VOLCANO ERUPTS
entities.summary: Lava rocks rain down and the ground splits open. There is no safe shoreline or corner: the damage arrives vertically first, then from below.
entities.howToGet: Shelter under solid cover beats running into the open, where falling rocks are unavoidable. Avoid standing over cracked ground once the splits start.
entities.banner: What if every volcano erupts at once?
stages: Lava rocks come down from above first, so the sky is the immediate threat.
The ground splits open underneath, which removes the ground-level answer.
Both continue together, so no single position stays safe for the whole round.
entities.killSpots: Open ground under falling rock, and standing over a crack when it opens. Unlike the tsunami, climbing does not fix this one — cover does.
prep: Get under something solid rather than high. This is the scenario where a roof beats a rooftop.
Avoid cracked ground as soon as it appears; it telegraphs where the splits run.
Plan one backup cover nearby — the first one gets hit eventually.
entities.ifCaught: Move under cover in short bursts and watch the sky between sprints. Crossing open ground in one run is what gets players hit.
entities.worstMaps: Jungle Pyramids and Alpine Ski Resort — open terrain with long sightlines and little roof cover.
entities.hud: The sound readout on the recorded round peaked at 47 with the sky filled — the rocks come down before the ground opens.

entities.name: AN EF5 TORNADO HITS YOUR STREET
entities.summary: The tornado destroys the buildings it passes through, so the map's cover is removed ahead of the damage rather than around it.
entities.howToGet: Watch the direction it is tracking and stay behind it - a building is only protection until the funnel reaches it. Never cross open ground in front of it.
entities.banner: What if an F5 tornado hits?
stages: The funnel tracks across the map and destroys the buildings it passes through.
Cover disappears ahead of the damage rather than around it, so the map changes as the tornado moves.
The path is the only thing that matters — being near it is survivable, being in front of it is not.
entities.killSpots: Any building on the funnel's path, and any open crossing in front of it. Players die by moving toward the next cover instead of away from the track.
prep: Find the funnel before you commit to a building, and stand behind it.
Do not use a building that sits directly on its line — it will not be there.
Keep a route that stays behind the track as it moves across the map.
entities.ifCaught: Run perpendicular to the track, not away from it in a straight line. Getting behind the funnel ends the threat; outrunning it does not.
entities.worstMaps: Suburban Neighborhood — the houses are the cover and the funnel takes the houses.
entities.hud: The readout says TORNADO FORMING… EF5, and the objective is STAY OUT OF THE STREET — the buildings are the shelter, the street is the funnel's path.

entities.name: All Ice Melts
entities.summary: Sea level rises and the heat scorches. The water takes the low ground first while the temperature works on everyone still outside.
entities.howToGet: Go up and stay dry, the same as a tsunami round - this one is slower, so there is time to get there properly.
entities.banner: What if all the ice on Earth melts?
stages: Sea level rises and takes the low ground first, the same way a tsunami round does but slower.
The heat turns lethal for anyone still outside, so the round is a race between water and exposure.
The shoreline keeps advancing, which means a position that is dry now is not dry at the end.
entities.killSpots: Low ground and open sun. This scenario gives you more time than a tsunami and punishes players who spend that time in the street.
prep: Go up early, the same as a water scenario — you have time to do it properly.
Prefer a position with shade or an interior for the heat half of the round.
Do not plan to come back down for anything.
entities.ifCaught: Climb and get indoors — both halves of this scenario are solved by the same move. Standing in the sun at street level loses to either one.
entities.worstMaps: Coastal Resort and Harbor Port for the water, Suburban Neighborhood for the exposure.
entities.hud: The stage that arrives with the water is A GIANT ICEBERG IS COMING; the recorded round was on Golden Gate, where the deck is the only dry line.

entities.name: The Greatest Solar Flare
entities.summary: Radiation fills the air, electronics die and rooftops melt. The roof that saved you in a tsunami is the wrong place here, because the top of the map is where the flare lands.
entities.howToGet: Get off the roof and into a building. Where the tsunami answer is up, this one is down and indoors.
entities.banner: What if the largest solar flare ever hits?
stages: The city goes dark first — the HUD stage reads THE CITY HAS GONE DARK: the last of the grid has failed and the sky keeps getting brighter.
The objective is GET INSIDE A BUILDING with a temperature readout climbing (34 °C in the recorded round).
Rooftops melt while the sky brightens, so the highest ground becomes the first thing lost.
entities.killSpots: Rooftops and open sky. This is the scenario that punishes the habit built by every water round: climbing first.
prep: Get indoors and stay low. Down is the answer here, not up.
Do not rely on anything powered once the flare starts.
If you are on a roof when the banner fires, spend the whole 30 seconds getting off it.
entities.ifCaught: Get under a roof immediately, even a low one. Distance from the sky matters more than the quality of the shelter.
entities.worstMaps: Any map where the only cover is a rooftop — the Golden Gate crossing has the least indoor space of any recorded map.

announced.name: A month of rain falls every few minutes
announced.note: Banner confirmed, hazard not documented yet.

announced.name: A city-killing asteroid
announced.note: Banner confirmed, hazard not documented yet.

announced.name: THE STORM WILL NEVER END
announced.note: Banner confirmed, described in-game as a tornado that never stops.

maps.name: Suburban Neighborhood
maps.note: Street-level houses, garages that open with the interact prompt and drivable cars. Vehicles hold several players at once, but a ride is never guaranteed.
maps.use: Two-storey houses with stairs are the height for water rounds; garages and cars are a fast reposition, but a passenger can be thrown off a moving car, so never treat a ride as the plan. Bus-stop shelters and car roofs count as height above the rising tide.

maps.name: Thrill Park
maps.note: Themed park map with landmarks that make it easy to recognise before the banner fires.
maps.use: Recorded with the mega storm, and the terrain explains why: long open walkways between structures, water rises through the whole zone, and structures get stripped by the wind.

maps.name: Alpine Ski Resort
maps.use: The most vertical map recorded, so it is the best one for a tsunami and the worst for an earthquake — the buildings shed and there is a lot of height to fall from.

maps.name: Coastal Resort
maps.note: Confirmed in creator footage; low shoreline makes water scenarios harder.
maps.use: The shoreline is most of the playable area, which makes it the worst case for every water scenario. Move inland before you move up.

maps.name: Harbor Port
maps.use: Docks and flat deck space: very little height and no roof cover. Water scenarios are close to unwinnable at deck level, so the plan is the nearest crane or warehouse roof.

maps.name: Golden Gate
maps.note: Bridge-style map seen in footage; the deck is the only way across.
maps.use: The deck is the only way across, which makes the crossing itself the hazard during a bomb, toxic air or flare round. Train carriages are the movable cover here.

maps.name: Jungle Temple Ruins
maps.note: Temple-and-jungle map recorded with the solar flare and the every-volcano round. Big pyramid steps give height, thin cover.
maps.use: Open terrain with long sightlines — good for seeing a tornado track, bad for a bomb or a flare. Height sits on the pyramids and the cover is thin.

maps.name: Tulip Windmill
maps.note: Windmill and field map recorded with the 1,000-year rain. Tall windmill structures are the height the round asks for.
maps.use: The windmill itself is the tallest building the rain round is looking for, so it is the right place to be — but the fields around it are the first thing to go under.

maps.name: Venice
maps.note: Canal city recorded with the planet flyby: water at street level and towers above it.
maps.use: Low interiors are the answer on this one — the flyby lifts what is above ground, and the canals leave little dry street to run along.

maps.name: Downtown City
maps.note: Dense street grid at night — the map the witching hour was recorded on.
maps.use: Short blocks mean you can always keep moving, which is the only answer to thorns. Ground level is the hazard, not the floor.

maps.name: Stadium District
maps.note: Stadium, forecourt and stands — recorded with the oxygen round.
maps.use: The stands are the upstairs the fire round asks for; the forecourt is the wide open ground where the fire front moves fastest.

maps.name: Hoover Dam
maps.note: Dam structure with a drop on one side — recorded late in a session.
maps.use: Very little roof cover but a lot of vertical structure, so it suits water and tilt rounds and punishes flare or bomb rounds.

maps.name: Starlight Drive-in
maps.note: Drive-in cinema lot with a screen tower — recorded with the magnitude 10 earthquake.
maps.use: The screen tower is the one tall structure; that makes it the high ground for water rounds and the worst place to be in an earthquake.

maps.name: Canyon Town
maps.note: Canyon settlement on several levels — recorded across a long session.
maps.use: Layered ground means there is always a higher shelf to reach, which suits water and lava rounds; the walls also block line of sight for tornado tracking.

guide.heading: The round loop, in order
guide.body: Lobby wait shows a NEXT DISASTER countdown next to the shop, settings, crates and leaderboards. Stand on the central pad before that timer hits zero - players on the pad are the ones who get loaded. Loading prints ENTERING SIMULATION, the map spawns you with DISASTER IN 00:30, and the disaster itself is only named when that countdown ends.

guide.heading: Use the 30 seconds, don't spend it
guide.body: Warm-up time is free movement, not free loot. On Suburban Neighborhood you can open garages and drive cars, and vehicles carry several players - but a ride is not guaranteed. The habit that survives rounds is using the head start to be somewhere defensible before the banner names the hazard.

guide.heading: Read the banner, not the map
guide.body: Disaster and map are chosen separately: the same map can host different scenarios, and the 'What if...?' banner is the only thing that tells you what is coming. Twenty-two scenarios have been recorded in-game, from a moon fall to a solar flare, and each one rewards a different position - up for water, indoors for the sun and the flare.

guide.heading: What credits are for
guide.body: Surviving pays credits, and credits buy equipment in the lobby shop. Crates are the other sink. Game passes are the Robux shortcut and are not required to survive rounds - several recorded rounds were won with starter equipment by moving early.

guide.heading: If you die
guide.body: Dead players spectate until the results banner, which reads X OF Y SURVIVED and lists survivors and casualties. Use that time on the next map instead of the current one: the disaster has already been decided.

gaps: The developer advertises more scenarios than the 22 recorded here; the exact current count has not been published as a list.
Only 7 of the advertised maps have been named in footage.
No codes exist as of 2026-10-25 - the lobby has SHOP, MISSIONS and INDEX, no code box.
The lobby INDEX button may be an in-game disaster index; its contents are still undocumented.
